articles.body: France braces for another weekend of unrest as the Yellow Vests return to the streets under the rallying cry of ‘Act III – Halloween’, with 70,000 police and security forces deployed after the riots and looting of recent weeks. A cash-strapped government faces mounting grievances, a rolling protest movement and little room for manoeuvre ahead of elections, as it struggles to restore order while grappling with crippling debt.
articles.headline: Halloween Protests & French Promises, US Mid Term Mood, What now for Israel?

articles.body: In tonight's show, the Senegalese capital is hosting the first Olympic event ever held in Africa, welcoming nearly 2,700 athletes for the 2026 Youth Olympic Games. Also, South Africa’s local elections are set for November 4, with the African National Congress facing growing pressure over its record in local government. And finally we are joined by Muse L'Artiste who's reconnecting to her roots with her latest EP Heritage bringing her father's compositions back to life.
articles.headline: First Youth Olympic Games in Africa

articles.body: Residents evacuated from the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky have left for Russia's Anapa city with a Ukrainian delegation, senior official David Arakhamia said Friday. They are expected to fly to Belarus before returning to Ukraine by bus, during a rare ceasefire brokered by the United States.
articles.headline: Residents leave Russian-occupied Oleshky in evacuation operation

articles.body: Almost 200 nations approved two agreements on Friday to halt biodiversity loss by 2030, following almost two weeks of negotiations that ran into extra time on the final day.
articles.headline: UN nature summit approves two key agreements after marathon negotiations

articles.body: Several social media accounts associated with sharing anti-immigrant views claim French Muslims were responsible for burning five churches on October 17 – the day the nation was rocked by en masse protests. But both this number and story are fictitious. The French government agency that monitors religious heritage sites confirmed only one fire in a church occured in recent days; its cause unknown.
articles.headline: 'Five churches set on fire by Muslims?' Fake news by Islamophobic social media accounts

articles.body: As the 2026 midterm elections approach, divisions within the MAGA camp are becoming increasingly visible. From the war in Iran and rising fuel prices to the Epstein files, several of Trump’s decisions are fuelling divisions among his most loyal supporters. Once united by a shared vision of America, MAGA now brings together factions that increasingly disagree over foreign policy, the economy and what “America First” should actually mean. Yet Trump remains the central figure holding this political coalition together – and he is fighting to keep it that way. Why are some of the president’s longtime allies distancing themselves from him? Can MAGA remain united despite these disagreements? And can Trump still mobilise his base ahead of the midterms? 🔍 Our journalist Stella Elgersma breaks down the divisions within the MAGA movement and Donald Trump’s strategy to rally his supporters, once again.
articles.headline: MAGA: Why Trump's movement is fracturing?

articles.body: Catherine Viette is pleased to welcome Jens Schumacher, Field Coordinator in Mykolaiv and Kherson with Solidarity International. Just a few kilometers separate the Ukrainian-controlled city of Kherson from Russian-occupied Oleshky. For civilians caught between military occupation, disrupted essential services and uncertain evacuation arrangements, geographical proximity offers little guarantee of access to life-saving assistance. Schumacher examines the humanitarian implications of a temporary ceasefire around Oleshky, where approximately 2,000 civilians were reported to remain. Although the cessation of attacks has created a limited opportunity for humanitarian operations, the geographical scope of the agreement, the prospects for evacuation and the possibility of sustained humanitarian access remain uncertain.
articles.headline: Oleshky: No access to basic needs, ceasefire offers limited opportunity for humanitarian assistance

articles.body: Russia’s most renowned independent newspaper, Novaya Gazeta, announced on Friday that it was ceasing publication after more than three decades. Known for its courageous investigative journalism, the flagship newspaper said the Kremlin’s crackdown and ban on the media outlet had made it impossible to continue its work.
articles.headline: Russia’s Novaya Gazeta to cease publication amid Kremlin crackdown

articles.body: We speak to the influential and long-serving president of the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU), Koen Lenaerts. The court is the EU's supreme judicial authority, responsible for ensuring that European law is interpreted and applied across all 27 member states.
articles.headline: 'The International Criminal Court deserves the Sakharov Prize': CJEU President Koen Lenaerts

articles.body: Some residents of Oleshky, a Russian-occupied town in southern Ukraine ravaged by food and medicine shortages, left on Friday during a rare ceasefire brokered by the United States – due to end on Sunday evening. Ukrainian and Russian officials visited the town together on Friday, delivering aid and marshalling those who wanted to leave.
articles.headline: Stranded locals use rare truce to leave Moscow-occupied town in Ukraine

articles.body: Russian made an unprecedented combative move this month as one of its military satellites, the Cosmos-2612, encroached upon the orbit of Ukrainian commercial satellite, Iceye-X36, in behaviour deemed "threatening" by the US State Department. Norbert Pouzin, an orbital analyst at French space tech firm, Aldoria, described the mercenary manoeuvre as the first of its kind.
articles.headline: Star Wars: Has Russia's war with Ukraine gone intergalactic?

articles.body: From the EU's perspective, the second Trump presidency has felt even more destabilising than the first. From making the false claim that the EU was set up to "screw" the United States, to slapping tariffs on European goods, to making territorial claims on Greenland, to doing a diesel deal with Vladimir Putin and telling Ukraine to get a new president, Donald Trump has more than ruffled feathers on this side of the ocean. He has shaken the very foundations of the historical transatlantic relationship.
articles.headline: Could US midterms impact the EU? Transatlantic ties hit new low after Trump-Putin diesel deal

articles.body: Carys Garland is pleased to welcome Renaud Foucart, Senior Lecturer at the Department of Economics ECARES at Lancaster University. An international dockworkers’ strike brings into focus the relationship between organized labor, technological change and Europe’s expanding military investment. Foucart argues that port workers’ strategic position in global supply chains gives them exceptional leverage: “They know how powerful they are.” While questioning their ability to redirect military policy, he expects that leverage to secure concessions on automation and working conditions: “They can get those concessions. And I think they will get them.”
articles.headline: French port strikes: Unions 'will get better working conditions', but can they curb militarisation?

articles.body: Starving and exhausted residents of Oleshky, a Russian-occupied town in southern Ukraine, were being evacuated on Friday, October 30, as part of a joint relief operation involving the opposing sides – the first operation of its kind in four years and eight months of war. FRANCE 24’s Ukraine correspondent Emmanuelle Chaze reports.
articles.headline: War in Ukraine: Evacuations under way in Russian-occupied Oleshky

articles.body: In France, thousands were protesting in the Paris suburb of La Verrière on Friday, a week after a racist terrorist attack killed one person and injured five others. The suspect, identified as Kevin T., admitted he was targeting people based on their appearance or religion and has been transferred to a Paris court. FRANCE 24's Morgan Ayre reports.
articles.headline: French crowd gathers for anti-islamophobia rally in Paris suburb after attack

articles.body: Cryptocurrency exchange giant Binance has been targeted by a record-breaking $6.3 billion cyber heist, with blockchain intelligence firms linking the attack to North Korea. By Thursday night in the US, a coordinated effort by major crypto platforms successfully froze roughly $3 billion of the stolen assets during a high-stakes race to track and secure the digital funds.
articles.headline: Biggest hack in history: Cryptocurrency giant Binance loses $6.3 billion

articles.body: A second day of mourning is underway in Spain, with some families still waiting for news about missing loved ones, following Wednesday's high speed train crash that killed 69 people. Some have flooded social media with desperate appeals for information, posting photos or describing the clothes their relatives were wearing when they boarded the trains.
articles.headline: Spain working to identify train crash dead as relatives' anguish grows

articles.body: According to one poll, 82 per cent of white evangelical Protestants voted for Donald Trump in the 2024 US presidential election. That makes pastor Caleb Campbell a significant outlier – he has been one of the few outspoken evangelical critics of the Trump administration, dating back to the president’s first term when he felt compelled to speak out against Trump’s plans to put “kids in cages” as part of an immigration crackdown. “I was told that I was possessed by a demon,” Campbell remembers. Now, as the midterms approach, he fears US politics and the current administration have become more distant than ever from the Bible’s teachings.
articles.headline: Midterms 2026: The former neo-Nazi pastor speaking out against Trump

articles.body: In an interview with FRANCE 24, former Israeli prime minister Ehud Barak said Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu "did not win" this week's election in Israel but "lost dramatically", and that his rival Gadi Eisenkot should ally with Arab parties. Barak also suggested that claims of Qatari funding for an Arab party aimed to distract from an ongoing corruption scandal, and warned that Netanyahu was ready to strike Iran to stay in power.
articles.headline: Israeli election: 'Netanyahu did not win, he lost dramatically,' former PM Barak says

articles.body: Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike said she remains in constant pain after surviving a botched lethal injection in September, in her first public statement since the failed execution. She expressed gratitude for those who saved her life while urging compassion for her victim's family.
articles.headline: 'Deeply hurt': Convicted murderer Christa Pike speaks out after botched execution

articles.body: Israel's wartime election appeared deadlocked on Tuesday, exit polls showed, ​with Gadi Eisenkot's opposition bloc running neck and neck with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's camp, leaving neither side with a clear path to power. The projections pointed to a setback for Netanyahu's coalition and potentially weeks of political wrangling to form a government. FRANCE 24's Jerusalem correspondent Noga Tarnopolsky has more.
articles.headline: Israel's election ends in deadlock as final results show no clear winner

articles.body: France's interior minister on Thursday warned of a "very high risk of public disorder" and announced the deployment of around 70,000 police officers for a new wave of protests this weekend. France has been rocked by widespread anger over the rising cost of living and inequality, with nationwide demonstrations on October 17 degenerating into some of the country's worst rioting in years. FRANCE 24's International Affairs Editor Rochelle Ferguson Bouyahi tells us more.
articles.headline: France braces for new wave of protests, govt warns of 'very high' violence risk

articles.body: A Greek container ship has sunk after being struck by three drones, potentially of Russian origin, in the Black Sea off the Bulgarian coast on Wednesday, October 28. This incident highlights growing concerns for commercial shipping as the conflict between Ukraine and Russia persists.
articles.headline: Black Sea shipping under growing threats as drones hit container ships

articles.body: In this edition of arts24, "Le Fantôme de l'Opéra" returns to French cinemas in a contemporary reinterpretation starring Deva Cassel and Romain Duris. We take a closer look.
articles.headline: 'The Phantom of the Opera' haunts French cinemas again

articles.body: TRAVERSE CITY, MICHIGAN — Michigan's Democratic coalition is fragmenting in real time days before a critical Senate election. After it seemed like former primary rivals Abdul El-Sayed and Rep. Haley Stevens might finally appear together, they’re back to sniping at each other. And it could hardly come at a worse moment as Democrats look to unite behind El-Sayed and hold on to a pivotal Senate seat. El-Sayed’s campaign is asking Stevens to stay away from all future campaign events in the closing days of the race, two people familiar with the decision, who were granted anonymity to discuss sensitive campaign dynamics, told POLITICO. She should stay away “as not to distract from the central issues of the campaign,” one of the people said. The brushoff capped a day of the two lobbing increasingly pointed statements back and forth at each other, frustrating Democrats who say the infighting risks imperiling a state the party can hardly afford to lose as they try to flip control of the Senate. “I have no idea what the hell Haley Stevens is doing. This is a moment where we have to recognize the stakes,” Michigan state Sen. Mallory McMorrow, who was squeezed out of the Democratic primary by the two other candidates, told CNN earlier on Friday, before El-Sayed issued his response. “People are not talking about ads. They are not talking about Haley Stevens. They are talking about the price of gas and groceries.” Stevens did not immediately respond to a question on if she will now stay off the trail, and did not respond to an earlier question about whether her appearance was contingent on him apologizing. El-Sayed’s campaign declined to comment. El-Sayed narrowly defeated Stevens in a bitter and hard-fought primary in August that exposed division over support for Israel. The seat now held by the retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters is crucial to Democratic hopes to take control of the Senate. Stevens and El Sayed have not campaigned together since a post-primary unity breakfast, but appeared on the verge of doing so earlier on Friday. Stevens initially said she would appear alongside El-Sayed and South Carolina Rep. Jim Clyburn at a church in Detroit on Sunday. But she said she expected the Democratic nominee to apologize for some of his past comments and condemn an ad run by an outside group supporting him that she described as antisemitic. The ad featured a conversation in a grocery store where a woman told a man they couldn't buy eggs because they had to set aside money for “killing Palestinians.” El-Sayed’s campaign had previously noted he was not affiliated with the ad. In response, El-Sayed did not touch on the ad or his past comments on Israel, instead saying that his campaign “has always been focused on addressing the most critical challenges Michiganders are facing” and that that focus “is why our people-powered campaign defeated a historic $70 [million] in outside spending from big corporations and AIPAC on behalf of Congresswoman Stevens.” “So while Congresswoman Stevens seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago, let’s all focus on the task at hand: that’s beating Mike Rogers,” El-Sayed said. Privately, Democrats are frustrated — some with Stevens. “Every Democrat was singing the same tune but now, because one person is tone deaf, the whole choir is thrown off,” said a Michigan Democratic operative who is not directly working for El-Sayed’s campaign. Some Democrats tried to downplay the fight heading into the final days of the race. “There’s been a lot of efforts to coalesce Democrats, both from Abdul and from the congresswoman. I think everybody's on the same page of Democrats just beating Mike Rogers," said Joe Tate, a state representative from Detroit who supported Stevens in the primary and is now backing El-Sayed. But he acknowledged that "when you have people that have competed through a primary, I know it can always have those lingering effects." Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg urged Democrats to come together to support El-Sayed. “I've never met somebody who I agree with on 100 percent of everything,” Buttigieg told reporters while campaigning in the state for House candidate Callie Barr on Friday. “But when our health care is at stake, when a chance to have a more affordable everyday life is at stake, the choice is clear: Mike Rogers has disqualified himself.” Republicans have sought to play up the Democratic divisions. Rogers, in a Friday evening post on X , called Stevens a “courageous leader” and said she was “absolutely right” to call on El-Sayed to apologize. “I agree with her and my campaign is about being there, showing up and defending these communities and all Michiganders,” Rogers said. President Donald Trump, at a Friday night rally in Daytona, Florida, had a characteristically blunt message: "If you're Black, or if you're Jewish, and you vote for Abdul, you're not smart,” he said. Stevens’ comments so close to the pivotal election left some Democrats wondering what her goal was. “If you are someone with a large platform — whether you are, say, an outgoing member of Congress or an out-of-state streamer — who genuinely wants Abdul El-Sayed to become the next U.S. Senator from the state of Michigan and for Democrats to take back the Senate and put a meaningful check on Donald Trump, before you speak publicly I would implore you to ask yourself ‘is what I’m doing actually helping, or am I just seeking attention?’,” Democratic operative Adam Carlson, who has polled for a pro El-Sayed super PAC, wrote on X . Sophia Cai contributed to this report.
articles.headline: El-Sayed campaign wants Stevens to stay away after day of back-and-forth sniping

articles.body: Democrats are poised for a good night next Tuesday. That doesn’t mean they’ve figured out how to win. More than a dozen lawmakers, campaign operatives, strategists and pollsters warned in interviews that national Democrats risk drawing the wrong conclusions if they take back control of at least one chamber of Congress next week. Those figures from across the party worry that the midterms, which have become a referendum on President Donald Trump, have done little to improve the Democratic Party’s brand. They caution that a favorable political environment has papered over persistent problems for a party still grappling with why it lost the 2024 presidential election. And they admit they are still sharply divided over what its message should be heading into 2028. “Don't confuse them losing with us winning,” said Morgan Jackson, the senior adviser to Democrat Roy Cooper’s Senate campaign in North Carolina. Cooper has consistently led in the polls by a wide margin in a state Trump won three times. “This is not an affirmation of the Democratic Party in any which way,” said one veteran Democratic pollster working on Senate campaigns, who was granted anonymity to speak candidly. “It is very much a rejection of Trump.” The Democratic Party’s approval rating plummeted in the aftermath of the 2024 presidential election, and remains relatively weak. That’s even as voters tell pollsters they are more likely to trust Democrats than Republicans on several fronts, including addressing the cost of living, which voters consistently say is their top issue this cycle. Democrats’ quest for a coherent, positive pitch to answer rising prices and perceived corruption in Washington has at times been stymied by infighting between the party’s progressive and moderate factions over the best way to respond to the Trump administration. Democrats fought over whether to prolong government shutdowns to protest funding for Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the slashing of health care subsidies in late 2025 and early 2026. They were quick to attack their own upon release of the Democratic National Committee’s formal autopsy on where the party went wrong in 2024. But as Americans soured on Trump’s agenda and the Iran war drove up costs, Democrats zeroed in on a broad “costs, chaos and corruption” message that blamed the White House — without having to resolve their own internal tensions and disorder. “When your opponent is destroying themselves," said Matt Barron, a Democratic strategist who has done work across the rural Midwest and Rust Belt, "just get out of the way and let it happen.” Nabbing wins in a midterm election with a historically unpopular president is one thing. Building a winning brand for a party that was soundly defeated at the polls just two years ago is another. “If all you do is say the other people are terrible, that only gets you so far,” said Democratic donor Oliver Libby, who has advised Democratic House candidates Cait Conley in New York and Johnny Garcia in Texas this cycle. “You can have a minimum viable product of a midterm with criticism. You definitely don't win a presidential year with just criticism.” In a new POLITICO Poll conducted by PF Global, more than half of Americans said if Republicans lose control of both the House and the Senate, it would be either because of Trump’s actions since he became president, or because Republicans have run weak campaigns. Just one in four said a Democrat-controlled Congress would be because the party had run a strong campaign. “There are people who are going to vote in this election who are going to vote against Republicans,” said Antjuan Seawright, a Democratic strategist and adviser to House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries. “That does not mean they are in love with Democrats. It just means they are voting against the people in charge.” Democratic strategist Lis Smith, an architect of Pete Buttigieg's 2020 presidential campaign, said the Democratic candidates performing well in historically deep-red territory are the ones distancing themselves from the national party. “That should tell party leaders something,” she said. Smith helped found the moderate groups Majority Democrats and The Bench, and is advising Democratic Senate candidates like Adam Hamilton in Kansas, James Talarico in Texas and Josh Turek in Iowa — all of whom have taken on that tack. In Kansas, Hamilton publicly asked former Vice President Kamala Harris to stay away from his campaign, and said he would vote against Chuck Schumer remaining the party’s leader in the Senate. In Texas, Talarico vowed to challenge the party’s “establishment” and “change the Democratic Party.” And in Iowa, Turek says he rarely thinks about the party, while Rob Sand, the Democratic gubernatorial candidate in the state, has said he wants to end the two-party system altogether. “The reality is that a lot of very average and even mediocre candidates get across the line in a wave election,” Smith said. “A wave can hide a lot of weaknesses, and so we need to be able to make sure that the party can survive when the wave recedes.” Assuming Democrats take back control of at least one chamber of Congress next week, top party operatives see an opportunity for their side to deliver for voters who have wanted more checks on the Trump administration’s expansive use of executive power. But many caution that Democrats on Capitol Hill should avoid leaning too hard into an anti-Trump message next year, while others argue that the anti-corruption message will continue to galvanize the electorate. "The thing that I would be concerned about, if you go from 2026 to 2028, is that people think that corruption, that elite control over our economy, is just a Trump issue," said Bill Neidhardt, who worked on Bernie Sanders’ 2020 presidential campaign and is now advising left-leaning Democratic candidate Will Lawrence and working to boost Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate for Senate in Michigan. “What they need to focus on is that corporate power, those billionaire elites who are dictating the terms of our economy, that's what people are upset with." William Garcia, the co-chair of Wisconsin’s La Crosse County Democratic Party, has been canvassing extensively for his party in the state’s rural-heavy 3rd district , where voters swung toward Trump in recent years . Democrats are now trying to claw back that support. “I think we’re going to have a great night on Nov. 3. And then all these Democrats are going to have to deliver on all of these things we’re talking about,” Garcia said. “If we get to the end of 2027 summer and we haven’t passed bills to make a substantial difference in people’s lives, that’s my biggest fear. We gotta deliver.” Others acknowledge that voters may hold the party to a higher bar if they succeed in taking back control of both chambers of Congress — and they’ll be ready to punish Democrats in 2028 if they don’t follow through on their campaign promises to hold the Trump administration to account and bring down the cost of living. It’s a slippery slope for a party that has historically struggled to convince voters that it is well equipped to handle the economy. In 2024, Trump persuaded the majority of voters they would be financially better off with him in the White House, while painting Democrats as a party more concerned with social issues. “If we start getting back into a party that cares more about non-economic issues, then we haven't learned the lesson,” warned Pete Giangreco, a veteran Democratic strategist who has worked on House, Senate and gubernatorial campaigns this cycle. “People just are going to keep hitting the change button until the economy starts working for them again.” Samuel Benson and Meredith Lee Hill contributed reporting.
articles.headline: 'A wave can hide a lot of weaknesses': Dems question if they'll learn anything

articles.body: POCONO RACEWAY, Pennsylvania — High up in the starting stand of a famed race track, Josh Shapiro waves a black-and-white checkered flag with an unmistakeable meaning: It’s over. The metaphor isn’t entirely accurate. “We may have a lead, but you're coming down this home stretch. People are nipping at your heels,” the Pennsylvania governor told POLITICO. “You’ve got to run hard.” Shapiro, the potential 2028 contender and 2024 veepstakes short-lister, does have reasons to be optimistic — and careful. He’s threatening a double-digit blowout over Stacy Garrity, a candidate backed by President Donald Trump, in the most important swing state in the nation. He’s also putting his coattails to the test. None of the other potential 2028 Democratic candidates has more at stake in their own backyard on Tuesday than Shapiro. He doesn’t have California Gov. Gavin Newsom’s map-breaking Proposition 50, designed to beat back the GOP redistricting, nor his platinum email list. He doesn’t have Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker’s billions or Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly’s deep bench of donors or former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg’s large map or the red-state credentials of Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear. Shapiro is on the brink of flipping four hotly contested congressional seats — and guaranteeing Democrats the House. Pennsylvania Democrats could also take control of the state Senate, including some heavily gerrymandered seats, giving the party a governing trifecta for the first time since 1992. “I’m not thinking about this as a victory for me,” he told POLITICO during a swing through the state. “I'm thinking about this as a victory for our country.” All of which paves the way for him to pass a $15 minimum wage and a raft of other measures that could buttress a 2028 presidential bid. Shapiro is very much following the Ron DeSantis theory of a presidential primary campaign: demonstrate dominance at home before branching out nationally — a strategy, it should be noted, that didn’t pay off for the Florida governor. “I think what really hurt DeSantis was that he decided he wasn't going to announce until after his legislative session, and that was May,” political strategist David Axelrod said. “Time is at a premium. If that’s his plan, that would be a miscalculation.” Will we see him venture beyond Pennsylvania’s boundaries before the end of the year? “I don’t know what my plans are,” Shapiro said. The day had the feeling of both an ending of one campaign and the beginning of another. Even as he urged a midday audience of about 100 people to vote for Paige Cognetti, the Scranton mayor running against Rep. Rob Bresnahan, and Brian Wrightson, the state Senate candidate challenging Sen. Rosemary Brown, he is nationalizing his rhetoric. “Don’t let Trump take away your hopefulness,” he told people gathered at East Stroudsburg University. “Don't let him make you feel pessimistic. Don't let him feel like change can't come or that we have to look in the rearview mirror for answers. The answers are always straight ahead.” Then there’s his set piece about the “American dream slipping away.” He’s broadening out his message beyond the commonwealth. “I think the work I do here in Pennsylvania, the confidence I give them about their government here can hopefully restore some of their faith in democracy, and I want in our democracy, and I want them to feel like they've got power to be able to shape the future of that American dream,” Shapiro told us. A few hours later, Shapiro materializes inside Salerno’s, a tavern in Old Forge known for its American cheese-topped pizza. He sets a room in which patrons already have had a few too many Rolling Rocks and pumpkin martinis abuzz. On the televisions, his own ad for Wrightson is playing on TV. He grips and grins and backslaps his way through the room. At the end of the bar, he picks up five pizzas for the road, ducks out the door and boards his bus for another Cognetti rally. Shapiro’s gubernatorial reelect isn’t drawing the buzz of some of the more razor’s-edge, online Senate races in the waning days of election season. But his project is no less remarkable. “If we can win enough seats here in Pennsylvania to change the balance of power in Washington and be a check on Donald Trump, then we can both hold the president accountable and get stuff done in Washington,” Shapiro says. “Likewise, here in Pennsylvania, if we can win a trifecta for the first time since Bill Clinton's election, I can raise wages almost immediately for tens of thousands of Pennsylvanians who are at or below minimum wage and raise wages for others. That's a concrete thing that we can accomplish.” At the raceway, he has just finished cutting a video racing around the Pocono Raceway’s Tricky Triangle when he flashes a grin. “I’ve got a surprise for you,” he says, inviting POLITICO to the starting stand above the storied three-turn NASCAR track in the Pocono foothills. Up the stairs, the burnt-orange fall foliage dances on the Pennsylvania horizon. It’s a vantage point Shapiro, as a NASCAR fan, has taken in many times. Despite the apt setting, he deflects when asked if he’s ready to announce the launch of his campaign. “If this is a metaphor,” he says, “it's for finishing the race strong.” There is just one wrinkle: Before he brandished the black-and-white flag, he picked up a green one, waving it vigorously. “I think you mis-saw that,” Shapiro said with a smile. “I was waving a checkered flag to finish the governor’s race.” Like this content? articles.body: This just in, according to new poll results: Americans don’t trust polls. Only 25% of Americans said political surveys correctly estimate votes, according to a new POLITICO Poll , conducted by PF Global. The result reveals that a significant portion of the public lacks faith in the industry as it contends with accusations of consistently failing to reach Republican voters. It comes amid an intensely scrutinized 2026 midterm cycle, where public polling and campaigns’ internal polls have shown many races within the margin of error in key battlegrounds and in once-safe red territory. Roughly one in four respondents say that polls showing a blue wave coming in November are wrong, and they expect Republicans to win key races. And 41% of Americans — including voters of both parties — either say polls tend to underestimate Democrats or that they tend to underestimate Republicans. There have been some high-profile blunders: Polls have missed the mark throughout the Trump era. This cycle alone, surveys in Democratic primaries incorrectly predicted that progressive Francesca Hong would win the race for Wisconsin governor and that Abdul El-Sayed — who did become Democrat’s Michigan Senate nominee — would win by a much wider margin than the 1 percentage point victory he eked out. Speaker Mike Johnson and other Republicans have cast doubt on the latest forecasts: The polls are “grossly underestimating Republican enthusiasm around the country,” Johnson said on Fox News this week, adding that “more and more Republicans are unwilling to participate in these surveys.” President Donald Trump has called the polls “fake” and “rigged.” Vice President JD Vance said he tells people to ignore the polls because they have a “demotivating effect on our voters.” Pollsters know their industry is facing heavy scrutiny. However: “There isn't another thing waiting in the wings to replace the full purpose of this tool,” said Charlotte Swasey, the director of analytics for the Democratic think tank Searchlight Institute, told POLITICO. “This is what we have, and it's difficult, it's increasingly difficult. But it's not dead by any sense of the word.” Pollsters have made a number of changes over the years — like capturing respondents across all levels of education attainment or adjusting their methodologies to account for low response rates among any given group.   Still, roughly two in five Americans who voted for Trump in 2024 say political polls tend to underestimate Republicans. Their feelings are not completely unfounded. In 2016, pollsters grossly underestimated support for then-candidate Trump, with most polls coalescing around a relatively secure victory for former Secretary of State Hilary Clinton. Distrust is especially widespread among Trump voters who identify as “MAGA Republicans” — his most loyal base. Three in five MAGA Trump voters say the polls indicating Democrats will win key races next week are incorrect. Among non-MAGA Trump voters, just a third feel the same. “National polls always underestimate support for Republicans,” said RNC national press secretary Natalie Baldassarre. “Polls may suggest one thing, but the American people get the final say, and Republicans remain laser-focused on driving voters to the polls, defying history, and protecting our majorities." “I do think that non-response among base Republican voters in some of these red states is a problem,” Christine Matthews, president of public opinion polling firm Bellwether Research, told POLITICO in a recent interview . Republican candidates and officials are banking on the non-response caveat as Senate races in states like Kansas, Mississippi and Nebraska — and to some extent, in South Carolina and Louisiana — all tighten, with less than one week until Election Day. If polling proves true, they could experience once-unthinkable losses in deep-red territory. But distrust is not limited to Republicans. Many in both parties were outraged after one group — Wedgewood Polls — admitted under scrutiny from FiftyPlusOne to using fake data in its polling results in several Democratic primaries, which some believe impacted election results . Another group published fake polling data on the Los Angeles mayoral race as a test to see how the data would travel before being verified. And just under a third of voters who backed former Vice President Kamala Harris say political polls tend to underestimate Democrats. Part of the distrust can come down to the fact that polls are not intended to forecast outcomes. They are a snapshot of public sentiment at a given point in time — and people can change their minds. One in five Americans said in POLITICO’s survey they have filled in a poll on how they would vote differently than how they actually voted. “Of course there are people who say something to a poll and then do something different a couple of weeks later,” said Seb Wride, head of polling at London-based PF Global, POLITICO’s polling partner. “I think it's quite possible that some of the races that were real big misses earlier this year were decided in the very last week.” According to a recent POLITICO survey, polls — which, when conducted correctly, involve careful planning and meticulous methodology — don’t earn much more trust than prediction markets, where odds are determined simply by bets placed by the public. Just 18% of people said they trusted poll-based forecasts over prediction markets to correctly predict the outcome of an election. That’s a marginal lead on the 12% of people who said they trust prediction markets over polls. A third said they trust neither. Still, most voters say they do make decisions based on polling. Roughly 55% of Americans say they would “definitely” go vote if the polls showed their preferred candidate far behind. Even among Republican midterm voters who say the polls underestimate their party, roughly 75% say the same. “There are a lot of voters that are motivated to send a message to the system,” said longtime GOP strategist Kevin Madden. “I think particularly on the [political] right, they'll be motivated to send a message, and essentially that message is ‘You're wrong, and the voters are right.’” The big question for campaigns is “are there enough of those?” he said.

articles.body: Republicans are bracing for a brutal election night, convinced they’re set to face some previously unthinkable losses in deep-red Trump territory as key battleground races hang on a knife’s edge . House Republicans are privately discussing not just if they’ll lose their majority, but by how many seats. Imperiled GOP incumbents in once safe districts have been begging party leaders for more money in the final few days to stem the bleeding, according to six people involved in internal conversations, granted anonymity to discuss them. Senate Republicans have found new cause to worry about contests in Ohio, Kansas and other red states. “It could be quite a brutal evening,” said one senior Republican involved in the private conversations, who like others in this article was granted anonymity to speak candidly. “Once the dominoes start falling it becomes hard to stop them.” Some Republican incumbents made an eyebrow-raising emergency decision. They stopped doing their own polling weeks ago as they tried to save every dollar for swaying voters as they begged for the GOP cavalry to arrive from President Donald Trump’s political operation to the National Republican Congressional Committee, according to three of the people. One Republican strategist working on midterm races simply responded to a question about the environment with a video of a dumpster on fire that was being swept away by flood waters. Top GOP officials and lawmakers have long known the political landscape would be bad, amid voter anger over the cost of living and aspects of Trump's policy agenda. But they’re facing a worse position than they expected earlier this year, with less than one week until Election Day. Republicans for weeks have worried that young men who’d voted for Trump, including white and Hispanic working class voters, will stay home amid disillusionment with high costs and the Iran war. That alone could allow Democrats to overperform in some areas after they hemorrhaged support among that voting bloc in 2024. At a Kwik Trip in Eau Claire, Wisconsin, this week in the hotly-contested 3rd District, Isaiah Romero was filling up his silver Ram truck. The 20-year-old said he cast his ballot for Trump in his first ever presidential election two years ago. His verdict on high fuel prices? “I think they’re bull,” he said as he looked over to the $6.39 per gallon diesel and $4.29 gas at the pump. Is he voting this time? “No,” Romero responded, adding: “I didn’t vote for this.” New fires have been popping up across the map just as soon as top GOP officials put out others. Trump canceled in-person rallies in deep-red Kansas and Iowa set for this weekend to instead hold a series of tele-rallies for GOP candidates in the final stretch. “Any Democrats telling you they aren’t winning the Senate [besides] a couple of seats are sandbagging expectations,” the senior Republican said. In Ohio, the race between GOP Sen. Jon Husted and former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown is still incredibly close in private and public polling. But Republicans have watched with horror as GOP governor nominee “Vivek’s [Ramaswamy’s] numbers have gone off a cliff” in the last few days after he ran an ad featuring Democrat Amy Acton’s estranged mother saying her daughter is a liar, according to the senior Republican and two others who saw the internal polling. Acton’s stepfather was charged with raping her when she was 12. The headwinds across all of Ohio are deeply problematic for Republicans. They now believe embattled Rep. Max Miller (R-Ohio) — who is facing child and domestic abuse allegations that he denies — will lose in a seat Trump won by double digits. South Carolina has become another unexpectedly nailbiting race for Republicans, where political newcomer Sen. Darline Graham is facing a well-funded Democratic challenger. But GOP operatives and officials are feeling somewhat better after outside groups injected cash into the race earlier this month and Trump announced another rally in the state to energize Republicans’ base. “It's a lot closer than I think we would ever want, but I think she's going to pull it out,” said Jeff Davis, chair of the Greenville County Republican Party. But in one of the most dire signs, once-unimaginable GOP worries have started to creep about deep-red Louisiana — where Trump announced this week he will hold an election-eve tele-rally for Senate nominee Julia Letlow. Speaker Mike Johnson, who is close with Letlow, will join as Republicans have grown wary about a surge of Black voters and other Democratic-leaning voters in early voting across the South. Senior Republicans believe Letlow will win, but they fear it will be by single digits if nothing changes. “The cakewalk turned into a knife fight,” said one Louisiana Republican who has talked with Letlow recently. “If Democrat turnout surges on Election Day, it’ll be a long night in Monroe,” the person added, and they expect Letlow to win by just 6 points in a state Trump won by 22 points two years ago. In another painful development for Republicans in Louisiana, GOP groups have even started an eye-popping spending war in a safe red gerrymandered seat — where a bitter Republican-on-Republican primary is unfolding between state Sen. Blake Miguez, who was formerly endorsed by Trump , and state Sen. Rick Edmonds, Johnson’s former pastor. Club for Growth poured another $220,000 into the race Thursday. Republicans fear the messy race is poised for a December runoff. "POLITICO's sad little rolodex of loser strategists have no idea what they're talking about, and if they really believe what they're saying they should come out of the shadows and put a name to their brain-dead comments,” said RNC spokesperson Natalie Baldassarre. “While Republicans have focused on real solutions to improve costs of living and make our nation safer, Democrats have nominated a gang of radicals who want to raise taxes, force everyone on government healthcare, and release criminals onto the streets,” said Joanna Rodriguez, spokesperson for the National Republican Senatorial Committee. On the House side, Republicans are bracing for a brutal night. But they’ve long been spending in some redder GOP districts to forestall a true disaster. Mike Marinella, a spokesperson for the NRCC, said that the committee worked in partnership with the campaigns and the RNC to launch coordinated advertising early in GOP-held districts not initially rated as competitive, including those represented by Reps. Jeff Hurd (Colo.), Bill Huizenga (Mich.), Rob Wittman (Va.), Mike Turner (Ohio), and Monica De La Cruz (Texas). The NRCC began airing coordinated ads in early August, more than a month before the DCCC. The NRCC also conducted polling in more than 100 districts, an eye-popping number, as they worked to see how far the fires had spread into red terrain and make sure they were moving resources where they were needed. Republicans still think they can unseat Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-Wash.) and Gabe Vasquez (D-N.M.), while flipping retiring Rep. Jared Golden’s (D-Maine) seat. But privately, Republicans believe North Carolina’s open 11th District is close to gone, as are several other deep-red seats Trump won by double digits, according to four people with knowledge of the situation. And they’re still not confident they’ll beat Rep. Don Davis (D-N.C.) in a seat the GOP thought would be an easy flip when they redrew it early this year. It’s become the most expensive House race in history. The Republican in Kentucky’s 6th district, where Trump won by 15 points in 2024, is barely hanging on, according to the four people. Even in the South Texas districts the GOP redrew in their favor, Republicans reached the point days ago where no amount of new money is going to change the upcoming catastrophe, said one Republican official involved in conversations about those races. Johnson traveled to Minnesota on Thursday to headline a fundraiser for GOP Rep. Brad Finstad, who Republicans are scrambling to shore up in a +12 Trump district. Finstad told POLITICO in an interview this week that he had warned senior Republicans for weeks about Democratic groups pouring money into the race in his southern Minnesota district. “We raised that with anybody and everybody that would want to hear it,” Finstad said. “From a global perspective, people were like, ‘Well, you won by 18, you’re fine.’ And, you know, those of us in Minnesota know that this district has always had kind of an independent streak to it.” Senate Democrats, meanwhile, are upbeat at their prospects, but public and private polling across close to the entire battleground map is running within the margin of error — meaning those states could break either way. “I would rather be us than them. But if anyone tells you they know what’s going to happen, they’re full of shit,” one senior Senate Democratic operative said. “Everything is close.” And some Republicans are taking solace in the fact that at least it’ll all soon be over. “I can see the light at the end of the tunnel,” said a GOP strategist working on a campaign that is trending toward Democrats. “It might be a semi-truck, but at least I can see it." Andrew Howard, Erin Doherty and Alec Hernández contributed to this report.

"></img><p>A las <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-29/un-error-humano-a-las-836-la-cadena-de-fallos-y-decisiones-con-las-que-el-gobierno-explica-la-nueva-tragedia-en-la-linea-madrid-sevilla.html" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-29/un-error-humano-a-las-836-la-cadena-de-fallos-y-decisiones-con-las-que-el-gobierno-explica-la-nueva-tragedia-en-la-linea-madrid-sevilla.html">8.31 del miércoles</a>, seis trenes que circulan por la línea de alta velocidad que une Madrid-Sevilla y se reparten por un tramo de 63 kilómetros se ven afectados por el mismo problema: se ha caído el sistema LZB, que sirve para que dos convoyes no coincidan en el mismo cantón o pequeño segmento de la línea. La consecuencia es inmediata. Todos se paran. Saben que van a tener que operar al amparo los sistemas ASFA (que mide la distancia entre trenes por balizas y es capaz de detenerlos si superan ciertas barreras de seguridad) y BSL (que se comunica con los trenes por señales en los laterales de la vía). Los maquinistas se ponen en contacto con el centro de coordinación de Adif en Atocha (Madrid), donde nadie parece sorprendido por la situación, <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-28/el-controlador-de-atocha-al-maquinista-del-ave-desconecte-y-vuelva-a-conectar-y-reanude-con-marcha-normal.html" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-28/el-controlador-de-atocha-al-maquinista-del-ave-desconecte-y-vuelva-a-conectar-y-reanude-con-marcha-normal.html">según los audios publicados por EL PAÍS</a>. En lo que va de año, el LZB ha dejado de estar en servicio en 170 ocasiones, según explica luego el ministro Óscar Puente. Eso supone que está desactivado casi una vez cada dos días, con incidencias de diferente duración. En este caso, la reactivación de la marcha, <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-30/los-controladores-de-atocha-ordenaron-seguir-el-protocolo-equivocado-antes-del-choque-entre-el-ave-y-el-iryo-me-estaba-liando.html" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-30/los-controladores-de-atocha-ordenaron-seguir-el-protocolo-equivocado-antes-del-choque-entre-el-ave-y-el-iryo-me-estaba-liando.html">para la que se aplican protocolos incorrectos</a>, lleva al desastre: un AVE lanzado a <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-29/el-primer-informe-tecnico-del-accidente-fija-en-160-a-200-kilometros-por-hora-la-velocidad-del-ave-que-choco-en-urda.html" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-29/el-primer-informe-tecnico-del-accidente-fija-en-160-a-200-kilometros-por-hora-la-velocidad-del-ave-que-choco-en-urda.html">entre 160 y 200 kilómetros por hora</a> percute contra un Iryo totalmente parado en Urda (Toledo), provocando al menos 69 muertos y centenares de heridos de diversa consideración. </p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-31/radiografia-del-sistema-de-seguridad-que-dejo-de-funcionar-antes-del-accidente-de-urda-casi-una-caida-cada-dos-dias.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p><img src="https://imagenes.elpais.com/resizer/v2/SDSHU25UP5DLDDNR4YRQSCPA6Q.jpg?auth=b8edf54010b48f673a24e419eb6c9dc15b13213762529fe3de76fdc36a85b0c5" width="3500" height="2334" alt="29/10/28 Día después del accidente de Ave e Iryo en Toledo, cerca de Urda. "></img><p>Todo el dolor del mundo cabe en el jardín arbolado que se extiende ante la<a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-30/70-familiares-esperan-la-peor-noticia-dentro-de-la-casa-parroquial-de-toledo-las-horas-que-pasan-nos-matan-nadie-nos-dice-nada.html" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-30/70-familiares-esperan-la-peor-noticia-dentro-de-la-casa-parroquial-de-toledo-las-horas-que-pasan-nos-matan-nadie-nos-dice-nada.html"> casa sacerdotal Buen Pastor de Toledo</a>, el lugar habilitado en la capital castellanomanchega para acoger a decenas de familiares de las víctimas desaparecidas. Aquí comen, algunos duermen y esperan noticias desde hace dos días. La gente charla en corrillos diseminados, en un ambiente en el que se mezclan la tristeza, la frustración, la rabia y la incertidumbre; las personas se abrazan de esa forma larga en la que a uno le da tiempo a acariciar la espalda del otro, se oyen durísimas conversaciones en voz baja —“Ella es pequeña, pero madura…”; “es bueno que pueda llevar una flor a una lápida”— y de vez en cuando se eleva un llanto desconsolado que provoca un nudo en el estómago. </p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-31/el-arzobispo-de-toledo-sobre-los-desaparecidos-del-accidente-de-tren-la-esperanza-no-quita-nada-del-dolor.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p><img src="https://imagenes.elpais.com/resizer/v2/HO7DQUPRMVEXTPQMWIV7LBDK2E.jpg?auth=d0cc820cdbb4299c93a5bdd5a2f746810ae71cb2ae96b1c970b4782415f7e7aa" width="1803" height="1089" alt="El arzobispo de Toledo, Francisco Cerro Chaves."></img>
articles.headline: El arzobispo de Toledo sobre los desaparecidos del accidente de tren: “La esperanza no quita nada del dolor”

"></img><p>Tres asociaciones y casi 70 particulares figuran ya como afectados en el procedimiento del Tribunal Supremo que ha derivado en la suspensión del voto para los nacionalizados por la <i>ley de nietos.</i> La Sala de lo Contencioso-Administrativo <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/elecciones-generales/2026-10-12/el-supremo-mantiene-para-el-29-n-la-suspension-del-derecho-al-voto-de-los-nacionalizados-por-la-ley-de-nietos.html" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/espana/elecciones-generales/2026-10-12/el-supremo-mantiene-para-el-29-n-la-suspension-del-derecho-al-voto-de-los-nacionalizados-por-la-ley-de-nietos.html">emplazó a personarse el pasado 12 de octubre</a> a los más de 163.000 nuevos españoles a los que ha retirado el derecho al sufragio, y, una vez terminado el plazo de cinco días abierto por el tribunal y examinadas todas las solicitudes, los jueces han aceptado la personación de 69 particulares y de la Asociación de Extranjeristas en Red, el Centro de Descendientes de Españoles Unidos (Cedeu) y la Asociación Pro Derechos Humanos de Andalucía, según la documentación a la que ha tenido acceso este periódico. Para todos ellos ha abierto un nuevo plazo de tres días para que presenten alegaciones sobre el procedimiento. </p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/elecciones-generales/2026-10-31/el-supremo-admite-a-69-personas-y-tres-asociaciones-como-afectados-por-la-suspension-del-voto-a-los-nacionalizados-por-la-ley-de-nietos.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p>
articles.headline: El Supremo admite a 69 personas y tres asociaciones como afectados por la suspensión del voto a los nacionalizados por la ‘ley de nietos’

articles.body: <p>Pedro Sánchez ha vuelto a incidir en que el accidente ferroviario de Urda, que deja de momento 69 fallecidos, cuestiona una infraestructura que hasta hace poco era un símbolo de modernidad, con el impacto que supone para la imagen del Estado. “Hay una confianza quebrada en el sistema de alta velocidad en nuestro país y la labor del Gobierno no es solamente hacer el diagnóstico, conocer cuáles son las causas, sino ofrecer soluciones para que una tragedia de esta magnitud, como ayer dijo el jefe del Estado, el rey Felipe VI, no vuelva a suceder”, ha afirmado en una comparecencia sin preguntas junto al presidente de Castilla-La Mancha, Emiliano García-Page, tras la reunión del Centro de Coordinación Operativa Integrado (Cecopi) en Toledo. </p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-30/sanchez-hay-una-confianza-quebrada-en-el-sistema-de-alta-velocidad.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p>
articles.headline: Sánchez: “Hay una confianza quebrada en el sistema de alta velocidad”

articles.body: <p>Falta de personal y una fuerte presión sobre los hombros de los operarios en horas pico de tráfico. Son dos de las quejas recurrentes de los sindicatos al referirse al Puesto de Mando y Centro de Regulación y Control (CRC) que el gestor de la infraestructura ferroviaria Adif tiene junto a la estación madrileña de Atocha. En él trabajan un centenar de personas en torno a Da Vinci, uno de los sistemas de vigilancia de la red ferroviaria más avanzados de Europa. Desde sus pantallas se monitoriza el control de tráfico centralizado, las comunicaciones fijas y GSMR, la señalización, sistemas de seguridad, sistemas de planificación y regulación del tráfico, videovigilancia y control de las estaciones. Hasta ahora, un motivo de orgullo para la compañía dependiente del Ministerio de Transportes, pero <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-29/la-guardia-civil-investiga-en-que-circunstancias-se-produjo-el-error-humano-del-accidente-de-urda.html" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-29/la-guardia-civil-investiga-en-que-circunstancias-se-produjo-el-error-humano-del-accidente-de-urda.html">es aquí donde se fragua la cadena de órdenes inconexas que acaban el miércoles en tragedia</a>, con <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-29/la-maquinista-del-iryo-de-urda-intento-desbloquear-su-tren-en-dos-ocasiones-sin-exito-y-busco-el-consejo-de-su-empresa-antes-de-la-colision.html" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-29/la-maquinista-del-iryo-de-urda-intento-desbloquear-su-tren-en-dos-ocasiones-sin-exito-y-busco-el-consejo-de-su-empresa-antes-de-la-colision.html">el choque de dos trenes</a> y al menos 69 víctimas, en la localidad toledana de Urda. </p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-30/centro-de-control-de-atocha-un-centenar-de-operarios-entre-la-presion-del-trafico-y-un-software-de-vanguardia.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p>
articles.headline: Centro de Control de Atocha, un centenar de operarios entre la presión del tráfico y un ‘software’ de vanguardia

articles.body: <p>“Es una pérdida enorme para toda España”. Eran las palabras del expresidente del Gobierno, Mariano Rajoy, en la despedida en San Juan del Puerto (Huelva) a la exministra popular Fátima Báñez, una de las 69 víctimas mortales del accidente ferroviario de Urda (Toledo). La parroquia de San Juan Bautista se ha quedado pequeña para acoger a los familiares, vecinos, dirigentes del PP, cargos de los gobiernos populares y amigos que han acudido a rendirle homenaje en una provincia que tiene muy presente las secuelas del accidente ferroviario de Adamuz, donde uno de los trenes siniestrados fue un Alvia que iba a Huelva. Menos de un año después, Fátima Báñez fue uno de los primeros nombres que se manejaron este miércoles como una de las posibles víctimas en el nuevo accidente. La terrible confirmación llegó el jueves tras pasar por el proceso de identificación del cadáver. </p><img src="https://imagenes.elpais.com/resizer/v2/BM2RWJONV5FE7KT5VYKUG5YYDQ.jpg?auth=b459400f9bc2e9c4a13c3d9ee2cde256bec1c6a49271f1ec650c85848a79a7f7" width="3150" height="2101" alt="Sepelio de la exministra Fátima Báñez en San Juan del Puerto (Huelva), este viernes."></img><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-30/dolor-y-emocion-en-la-despedida-de-familiares-vecinos-y-dirigentes-del-pp-a-fatima-banez-en-san-juan-del-puerto.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p>
articles.headline: Dolor y emoción en la despedida de familiares, vecinos y dirigentes del PP a Fátima Báñez en San Juan del Puerto

articles.body: <p>El Tribunal Supremo estudiará <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/elecciones-generales/2026-10-28/el-gobierno-entrega-al-supremo-la-lista-con-los-nacionalizados-por-la-ley-de-nietos.html" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/espana/elecciones-generales/2026-10-28/el-gobierno-entrega-al-supremo-la-lista-con-los-nacionalizados-por-la-ley-de-nietos.html">si suspende también el derecho al voto de los hijos de los nacionalizados</a> por la <i>ley de nietos</i> a los que se ha retirado el sufragio para el 29-N. La Sala de lo Contencioso-Adiministrativo descarta adoptar esta medida por la vía urgente, pero en una resolución dictada este viernes, ha dado tres días a las partes para que se pronuncien sobre la petición formulada por Iustitia Europa, que reclama que la medida adoptada por los jueces para más de 163.000 nacionalizados como hijos o nietos del exilio se extienda a su vez a los descendientes de estos, nacionalizados por otro apartado de la Ley de Memoria Democrática que no está afectado por la suspensión del voto acordada por el Supremo. Según los datos de Exteriores incorporados al procedimiento por la Abogacía del Estado, por ese supuesto se han nacionalizado más de 189.000 personas que ya están inscritas en el censo de extranjero.</p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/elecciones-generales/2026-10-30/el-supremo-estudiara-si-suspende-tambien-el-voto-de-los-hijos-de-los-nacionalizados-por-la-ley-de-nietos.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p>
articles.headline: El Supremo estudiará si suspende también el voto de los hijos de los nacionalizados por la ‘ley de nietos’

articles.body: <p>Las fuerzas de seguridad españolas han detenido este viernes, de momento, a ocho jóvenes, uno de ellos de 16 años, por su vinculación con <i>Blocus. </i>Este movimiento<i> </i>localizado en las redes sociales ha convocado este sábado a sus seguidores para provocar disturbios y cometer saqueos en los comercios de distintas ciudades, coincidiendo con la noche de Halloween, el 31 de octubre. </p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/comunidad-valenciana/2026-10-30/detenido-un-segundo-miembro-de-blocus-valencia-por-instigar-a-fabricar-y-arrojar-cocteles-molotov.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p>

articles.body: <p>Alberto Núñez Feijóo ha cambiado el paso y ha acusado este viernes directamente al Gobierno de ser el responsable de las muertes de <a href="https://elpais.com/noticias/accidente-ferrocarriles-urda-2026/" target="_blank" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/noticias/accidente-ferrocarriles-urda-2026/">los dos accidentes ferroviarios de este año en Adamuz y Urda</a>. “Han muerto 46 personas por un mantenimiento deficiente por parte del Gobierno en Adamuz, y al menos 69 en Toledo porque no renovó un sistema de seguridad obsoleto cuando debería haberlo hecho”, ha afirmado en una comparecencia en la sede del PP tras una reunión con expertos en el sistema ferroviario. El líder del PP ha responsabilizado al Ejecutivo de la tragedia,<a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-30/ultima-hora-y-reacciones-tras-el-accidente-de-trenes-de-urda-toledo-en-directo.html" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-30/ultima-hora-y-reacciones-tras-el-accidente-de-trenes-de-urda-toledo-en-directo.html"> y no solo al ministro de Transportes, Óscar Puente, que este viernes ha descartado dimitir, </a>sino también al presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez. “Quien ha faltado a su deber de gestionar con seriedad el Ministerio de Transportes tiene que cargar con ello. Ahora bien, quien lo ha nombrado y lo ha mantenido, con más motivo”, ha acusado el líder popular. “Si no dimiten ellos, les dimitiremos en las urnas”.</p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-30/feijoo-apunta-al-mantenimiento-deficiente-de-la-alta-velocidad-si-no-dimiten-ellos-los-dimitiremos-en-las-urnas.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p>
articles.headline: Feijóo: “Han muerto 69 personas porque el Gobierno no renovó un sistema de seguridad obsoleto”

articles.body: <p>El operador del Centro de Regulación y Control (CRC) de Adif en Madrid-Puerta de Atocha que autorizó a <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-30/las-llamadas-entre-atocha-y-los-maquinistas-explicadas-paso-a-paso.html" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-30/las-llamadas-entre-atocha-y-los-maquinistas-explicadas-paso-a-paso.html">retomar la marcha al tren AVE de Renfe que embistió a un convoy de Iryo</a> el miércoles en Urda (Toledo) se acogió el jueves por la tarde a su derecho a no declarar ante los agentes de la Guardia Civil que le convocaron para interrogarlo, según detallan fuentes conocedoras del avance de las pesquisas. El trabajador había sido citado en calidad de investigado no detenido para que pudiera comparecer acompañado de abogado. Durante la lectura de sus derechos, se le preguntó si quería responder voluntariamente a las preguntas que se le iban a formular, y él dijo que no. Con ello, se dio por terminada su comparecencia. Es previsible que la jueza de Orgaz (Toledo) que instruye la causa, Aristea Ortiz, lo cite en los próximos días para tomarle declaración.</p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-30/el-operador-que-autorizo-al-ave-a-retomar-la-marcha-se-acoge-ante-la-guardia-civil-a-su-derecho-a-no-declarar.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p>

articles.body: <p>El presidente de Castilla-La Mancha, Emiliano García-Page, ha informado tras la reunión del Centro de Coordinación Operativa Integrado (CECOPI) que la cifra de víctimas mortales que se puede comunicar sigue siendo de 69, pero no descarta que aumente. <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-30/70-familiares-esperan-la-peor-noticia-dentro-de-la-casa-parroquial-de-toledo-las-horas-que-pasan-nos-matan-nadie-nos-dice-nada.html" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-30/70-familiares-esperan-la-peor-noticia-dentro-de-la-casa-parroquial-de-toledo-las-horas-que-pasan-nos-matan-nadie-nos-dice-nada.html">“Hay 70 denuncias de desaparecidos,</a> no descartamos que pueda haber más fallecidos”, ha explicado en una comparecencia junto al presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez. “Lo que aparece en los depósitos son 68 cadáveres completos, más el fallecido en hospital y los restos que están en un proceso muy complejo de identificación”, ha detallado el presidente autonómico.</p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-30/page-avisa-de-que-hay-muchos-restos-sin-identificar-y-no-descarta-que-aumente-la-cifra-de-fallecidos.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p>

articles.body: (ACN) Sota el lema “Prou privatització de l’habitatge públic”, un centenar de persones s’han concentrat aquest divendres a la plaça de Sant Jaume per reclamar que la promoció i la gestió de l’habitatge públic es mantingui en mans d’entitats sense ànim de lucre . La convocatòria està dirigida a l’Ajuntament de Barcelona, a qui demanen que s’aturin els concursos municipals oberts a promotors privats que preveuen construir més de 1.000 pisos en sòl públic. “La titularitat pública del terreny és necessària, però també importa qui gestiona els habitatges i on van els diners que paguen les persones que hi viuen “, asseguren des de la Xarxa d’Economia Solidària de Catalunya, XES, que ha convocat aquesta mobilització. En aquest sentit, consideren que els privats fan lucre “durant dècades”, fins i tot quan ja s’ha pagat la promoció. Per això afirmen que aquest sistema “comparteix la lògica del model d’Ayuso a Madrid “, en el qual el sòl públic es posa a disposició de negocis privats de lloguer. Més terrenys per a entitats cooperatives Per altra banda, la XES ha defensat que les entitats socials farien una millor gestió d’aquests habitatges públics perquè “abaixen les quotes amb el temps, tenen millor cura de les instal·lacions i mantenen edificis de més qualitat”. Per aquest motiu han exigit “aturar els concursos oberts al lucre privat”, i signar l’ampliació del Conveni ESAL per cedir solars a les entitats cooperatives. Aquesta firma podria impulsar la construcció de 2.000 habitatges fins al 2030 . Foto: Aina Martí (ACN) Un conveni per garantir més habitatge assequible De fet, la concentració havia de coincidir amb el ple municipal d’aquest divendres, però aquest s’ha ajornat pels tres dies de dol que es van decretar arran de l’accident de Toledo. En el ple d’aquest divendres, concretament, s’havia de votar la cessió de dos solars per construir 112 habitatges protegits. Segons la XES, el conveni ESAL és una fórmula “insuficient però d’èxit”, i per això consideren que no es poden quedar “de braços plegats”. Concretament demana que s’aturin tres concursos , convocats entre el desembre del 2024 i el juliol del 2026, que preveuen la construcció de 1.032 habitatges en conjunt.

articles.body: L’ acampada de la plaça de Catalunya ha assegurat que mantindrà la protesta malgrat la convocatòria de Blocus per aquest dissabte i les amenaces rebudes per part de grups ultres. En una roda de premsa coincidint amb el primer mes de mobilització, els activistes han reiterat que continuaran a la plaça i han defensat el caràcter pacífic del moviment. Els acampats han afirmat que no tenen previst canviar l’estratègia seguida fins ara. Han explicat que mantindran els controls d’accés habituals durant la nit, amb el recinte perimetrat i han insistit que rebutgen qualsevol resposta violenta. “No tenim cap tipus de por, ens mantenim aquí” , ha assegurat Amar, un dels membres del col·lectiu. També ha insistit que el moviment continuarà sent “pacífic” i ha descartat qualsevol resposta agressiva. Tampoc no se’ls ha traslladat cap dispositiu especial ni cap consigna concreta relacionada amb la mobilització prevista. L’acampada també ha denunciat que en les darreres setmanes ha rebut “amenaces feixistes” i ha reclamat a l’Ajuntament de Barcelona que restitueixi l’enllumenat públic de la plaça. Per això, han advertit que no abandonaran la mobilització fins que les administracions garanteixin recursos i alternatives per a les persones que actualment hi troben suport. En aquest sentit, l’acampada ha expressat la voluntat de dialogar amb les administracions. Ara bé, els activistes també han remarcat que només marxaran quan hi hagi solucions que considerin efectives. “No ens aixecarem fins que no ens donin solucions tangibles” , ha remarcat Kiera Monroy.

articles.body: El club de futbol Atlètic Hostafrancs torna a competir una dècada després de la seva desaparició. Més enllà del retorn d’un equip al terreny de joc, la refundació d’aquest club representa el compliment d’una il·lusió col·lectiva . I també un somni personal per al Marc Toyas, president actual del club i un dels joves futbolistes que van vestir la samarreta de l’entitat ara fa 10 anys , quan era tot just un adolescent. “Sempre he estat vinculat al club per amistat de la meva família amb persones que portaven l’entitat, des de ben petit. Per a mi, aleshores anar a veure l’Atlètic d’Hostafrancs era com a anar a veure el Barça “, recorda el Marc a l’ Infobarris . Recuperar el llegat d’un club fundat l’any 76 Fundat l’any 1976 , l’Atlètic Hostafrancs era un equip amateur . La manca d’un relleu generacional i de recursos humans va obligar a tancar-lo l’any 2016. “L’entitat va quedar adormida, però amb el somni de despertar-la “, recorda el president. De fet, fa anys que ell perseguia aquest objectiu. “Era una llàstima que es perdés i des del moment que em van dir que la temporada següent no seguiríem ja vaig començar a pensar què fer”. I la idea de la refundació del club va començar a prendre forma seriosa fa cinc anys. “Ara farà gairebé 50 anys d’història , i volem donar al barri d’Hostafrancs una altra vegada un club de futbol que no teniu un referent esportiu . Soc veí d’Hostafrancs i em sento aquest barri com el que és: casa meva”, afirma el Marc Toyas. El Primavera Sound, implicat en la refundació L’Atletic Hostafrancs ha topat amb una molt bona acollida amb les entitat del barri. “Hi ha gent propera que ja sabia que tenim experiència, ens vam reunir amb ells i els va encantar la idea”, recorda. Per a la posada en marxa i el finançament han tingut el suport de la Fundació Primavera Sound . “Sabem que fan projectes socials i treballen per no perdre la identitat de barri. Els vam plantejar el projecte i com que són futbolers també els va agradar i estan molt predisposats a donar-nos un cop de mà en aquest inici”, comenta el president. La magrana, a l’escut L’arrelament amb el barri es reflecteix també en els colors i l’equipació del club. La samarreta manté els colors vinculats històricament a Hostafrancs i recupera la magrana com a símbol , ja present en l’escut original. “La idea no era crear un club de nou, sinó refundar el que ja existia”, subratlla. A tot plegat han afegit l’any de la fundació. A contrarellotge el club va aconseguir completar tots els tràmits necessaris per poder inscriure l’equip a Quarta Catalana la primavera passada. Per entrenar, disposen d’un dels camps del la Ciutat Esportiva del CF Damm , i els partits els juguen al camp Municipal Futbol Iberia . Un camp més proper per poder créixer El principal repte és ara apropar el terreny de joc al barri. “És un anhel de tots els clubs de Sants-Montjuïc, acostar-nos més a la zona de Sants, Hostafrancs i la Bordeta “, comenta. Aquest lloc esperen que sigui el futur camp de la Magòria , en projecte. El proper pas per al club és crear un primer equip femení . “Creiem en el futbol femení i volem que surti aquest equip, però dependrà de disposar un camp municipal que ens permeti afegir més categories”, assenyala. A més llarg termini tenen previst incorporar el futbol base . Un inici de temporada complicat L’Atlètic Hostafrancs ha començat la temporada a contrarellotge i, per això, ja preveia un inici complicat . “Seguim construint l’equip, com volem que sigui el nostre model de joc . És complicat trobar jugadors que es compenetrin ràpidament”, explica. Tot i que l’inici ha estat fluixet, la il·lusió del club segueix intacte. “Sabem que sobretot la primera volta serà complicada , hi ha equips que porten molts anys junts”, assenyala. Amb aquesta realitat assumida, el club afronta aquesta primera temporada amb paciència i amb la intenció de lluitar en nom de tot un barri. articles.body: Després de vèncer aquest dijous a la pista del Skanderborg danès, el Barça ja sap quins seran els seus contrincants a la ronda principal de la màxima competició continental d’hanbol. Entre d’altres rivals, els blaugrana jugaran amb el Magdeburg o el Kielce . L’equip blaugrana d’handbol ha conegut aquest divendres els propers rivals a la Lliga de Campions per la ronda principal. Jugarà els 10 partits d’aquesta fase de la competició entre el 19 de novembre i el 3 o 4 de març. Aquesta ronda consisteix en dos grups de sis equips, i el Barça haurà de lluitar per accedir els quarts de final. Per aconseguir aquest objectiu, haurà de classificar-se entre els quatre primers. De fet, el Barça debutarà a la main round a la pista del Kielce aquest 19 de novembre a les 18.45 h. El primer partit d’aquesta fase al Palau Blaugrana serà contra el GOG danès. Acabarà la segona ronda de la Champions al Palau contra el Kielce la setmana del 3 de març, encara sense confirmar ni data no hora. L’equip blaugrana va guanyar tots els partits del seu grup i va accedir a la main round com a líder. Precisament, en el grup de la segona ronda de la Champions s’ha tornat a emparellar amb el Dinamo de Bucarest , però com que ja es van enfrontar en l’anterior i el Barça va guanyar l’equip romanès per partida doble, 22-36 a Bucarest i 34-27 al Palau, els de Carlos Ortega començarà aquesta main round com a líders amb quatre punts sense la necessitat de tornar a veure les cares al Dinamo.

articles.body: (ACN/Redacció) L’Autoritat Catalana de la Competència (ACCO) demana preservar l’oferta del servei de bicicletes de lloguer compartit a Barcelona que l’Ajuntament vol eliminar el 2027 . En un document publicat aquesta setmana, ha alertat dels efectes que podria tenir la mesura. L’ACCO adverteix que reduiria les alternatives de mobilitat disponibles , eliminaria la pressió competitiva sobre el servei municipal de Bicing i afebliria els incentius a millorar preus, qualitat o innovació. Des de l’Ajuntament assenyalen que estan estudiant el document de l’ACCO, però insisteixen que la decisió de no renovar les llicències de bici compartida es basa en l’incompliment reiterat de les condicions de la concessió i de l’impacte en l’espai públic. També et pot interessar Barcelona eliminarà les bicis compartides el 2027 pel “desgavell i mal ús” que en fan els usuaris Roger Torres i Liñán 1 minut de lectura Fer una rova regulació Tot i això, l’ACCO insta l’Ajuntament a propiciar una nova regulació que faciliti la convivència del Bicing amb altres operadors . Competència recorda que el consistori actua simultàniament com a regulador de l’activitat i com a titular del servei municipal. Per aquesta doble condició, l’organisme exigeix una “especial cautela per evitar que les decisions reguladores introdueixin avantatges injustificats” a favor de la titularitat pública. Així mateix, assenyala que l’ampliació del Bicing no ha de preservar per si mateixa els beneficis associats a l’oferta de diversos prestadors del servei de bicicleta compartida. Així apunten que aquest estiu passat s’han batut rècords mensuals de sancions imposades i de vehicles ingressats al dipòsit municipal per dificultar el pas i la circulació. articles.body: Quan escrivim hi ha paraules que ens porten pel pedregar perquè en singular no porten accent però en plural, sí . És el cas dels mots fenomen , examen i origen . També et pot interessar “Soc” o “sóc”, un dubte existencial btvllengua 1 minut de lectura Un fenomen que no és singular Les paraules fenomen , examen i origen no s’accentuen, però en plural, fenòmens , exàmens i orígens , sí. El motiu: en singular no porten accent perquè són paraules planes acabades en -en , però quan les pluralitzem canvia la terminació. Com que ara acaben en -ns i les paraules planes acabades en aquesta terminació sí que s’accentuen, hi hem de posar l’accent gràfic. fenomen → fenòmens examen → exàmens origen → orígens Per entendre-ho més bé, farem un repàs de les regles d’accentuació. Accentuació de butxaca Primer definim, després accentuem: Un mot és agut quan la síl·laba tònica és l’ última . Un mot és pla quan la síl·laba tònica és la penúltima . Un mot és esdrúixol quan la síl·laba tònica és l’ antepenúltima .
